title: Κάμηλος καὶ Ζεύς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 146. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κάμηλος θεασαμένη ταῦρον ἐπὶ τοῖς κέρασιν ἀγαλλόμενον, φθονήσασα αὐτῷ, ἐβουλήθη καὶ αὐτὴ τῶν ἴσων ἐφικέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Kamēlos theasamenē tauron epi tois kerasin agallomenon, phthonēsasa autōi, eboulēthē kai autē tōn isōn ephikesthai.
sentences.l: A camel, having beheld a bull glorying in his horns, having envied him, wished herself too to attain the same.
sentences.i: A camel, seeing a bull glorying in his horns, envied him and wished to come by the like herself.
sentences.n: κάμηλος is feminine here, as the participles θεασαμένη and φθονήσασα show. φθονέω takes the dative of the person envied. ἐφικνέομαι, "reach as far as, attain", takes the genitive of what is reached: τῶν ἴσων, "the equal things", the same equipment the bull has.

sentences.t: Διόπερ παραγενομένη πρὸς τὸν Δία, τούτου ἐδέετο, ὅπως αὐτῇ κέρατα προσνείμῃ.
sentences.tr: Dioper paragenomenē pros ton Dia, toutou edeeto, hopōs autēi kerata prosneimēi.
sentences.l: Wherefore, having come to Zeus, she begged of him that he assign her horns.
sentences.i: And so she went to Zeus and begged him to grant her horns.
sentences.n: δέομαι, "ask, beg", takes the genitive of the person asked (τούτου). ὅπως with the subjunctive after a verb of entreaty states the thing aimed at. προσνέμω is "assign, allot to", the προσ- pointing to the person the share is given to.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ Ζεὺς ἀγανακτήσας κατ’ αὐτῆς, εἴγε μὴ ἀρκεῖται τῷ μεγέθει τοῦ σώματος καὶ τῇ ἰσχύι, ἀλλὰ καὶ περισσοτέρων ἐπιθυμεῖ, οὐ μόνον αὐτῇ κέρατα οὐ προσέθηκεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ μέρος τι τῶν ὤτων ἀφείλετο.
sentences.tr: Kai ho Zeus aganaktēsas kat’ autēs, eige mē arkeitai tōi megethei tou sōmatos kai tēi ischyi, alla kai perissoterōn epithymei, ou monon autēi kerata ou prosethēken, alla kai meros ti tōn ōtōn apheileto.
sentences.l: And Zeus, having grown vexed against her, if indeed she is not content with the size of her body and with her strength, but desires yet more besides, not only did not add horns to her, but even took away some part of her ears.
sentences.i: And Zeus, indignant at her — that she was not content with the size of her body and her strength, but craved more besides — not only refused her horns, but took away part of her ears as well.
sentences.n: κατά with the genitive after a word of anger is "against". εἴγε keeps the god's own reasoning in the indicative, as though we overheard the ground of his displeasure. ἀρκέομαι takes the dative of what contents one, ἐπιθυμέω the genitive of what is craved. ἀφείλετο is aorist middle, and the middle of ἀφαιρέω is simply the ordinary way of saying "take away from, deprive of" — it does not mean Zeus wanted the ears. The camel is left worse off than she began.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ διὰ πλεονεξίαν τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐποφθαλμιῶντες λανθάνουσι καὶ τῶν ἰδίων στερούμενοι.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi dia pleonexian tois allois epophthalmiōntes lanthanousi kai tōn idiōn steroumenoi.
sentences.l: Thus many, through greed casting their eyes upon others, fail to notice that they are being robbed even of what is their own.
sentences.i: Thus many, in their greed eyeing what others have, lose even what is their own before they know it.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle carries the weight the other way round from English: the participle (στερούμενοι) holds the real action and the verb says only that it went unobserved. ἐποφθαλμιάω, "to set the eye upon", takes the dative. στερέομαι takes the genitive of what is lost, and καί before it is "even".
